extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers and worldbuilders (novelists, short-story authors) looking for tools and organizational strategies
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical criteria for choosing tools and organizing worldbuilding and manuscript material (timelines, character info, continuity) during fiction writing. Covers software, analog tools, workflows, and collaboration practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose tools that fit who you are
rubrics_metrics.description: "I think the best tools are ones that kind of work with who you are and shore you up where you might need more support."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select tools that compensate for your weaknesses and match your process (e.g., PowerPoint for visual thinkers; a minimal word-processor environment for writers who want a typewriter-like experience). Trying to force a workflow that doesn't suit you will reduce effectiveness. Examples given: PowerPoint used as a visual world/reference board; Dan turns off features to make his word processor act like a simple typewriter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a world bible / single reference place
rubrics_metrics.description: Have one place (or clearly organized set of files) where you put character traits, locations, technology, and other recurring world details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'world bible' can be implemented in Scrivener, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, a wiki, a set of notecards, or multiple files — whatever makes the material findable and usable. Label and organize entries so you can retrieve them quickly when writing. Mary Robinette, Dan, and others describe different implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on worldbuilding elements that actually impact the story
rubrics_metrics.description: "If it’s not in the novel, then it’s not canon." Decide which worldbuilding details affect characters or plot and prioritize tracking those.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review your stored material and identify which elements influence character journeys or scenes; deprioritize 'fun' but irrelevant backstory. This reduces clutter and emphasizes findability of story-relevant facts. Erin suggests identifying five favorite elements and tracing their influences to ensure they're purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track mundane details as well as the exotic
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember to record the everyday or mundane features of the world (topsoil, ordinary rocks, sinks) because these are often forgotten and can cause inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mundane elements may be less interesting to invent but are essential for believable continuity; explicitly note them in your bible or reference documents so you don't accidentally portray the world as 'only the interesting bits.' Example: Dan forgetting that an alien planet has actual dirt amid large crystals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use search and indexable references to maintain consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: "I use the search function." Use searchable terms and index inventions so you can find them quickly in your manuscript or notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For invented or hard-to-spell words, jot them down in an index so searches will find all instances. Use program search tools (Word, Scrivener, editors) to locate occurrences and check consistency of names, terms, and facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ version control / snapshots / cloning
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep versions, snapshots or clones of scenes so you can try big changes without losing prior text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrivener features: clone scenes, take snapshots on revisions, use a 'scraps' folder for discarded content. This lets you compare alternate versions and recover deleted material. Alternative workflow: some writers prefer deleting and rewriting; choose what sparks productivity for you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chunk material so you can reorder easily
rubrics_metrics.description: Break manuscript into chunks (chapters, scenes) that can be moved and reorganized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools that support chunking (Scrivener's binder, notecards, physical index cards) make it simple to rearrange structure. Chunking helps you see shape and flow and to test alternative scene orders quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use timelines and calendars for temporal consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Use timeline tools or physical calendars to plan and verify sequences of events and time-of-day details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include Aeon Timeline, Excel timeline sheets, printed historical calendars (e.g., Mary printed a 1963 calendar), or dedicated timeline software. Divide days into parts (morning, afternoon, night) where helpful. Timelines prevent errors in event ordering and time-of-day continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spreadsheets (Excel) for structured tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Excel or spreadsheets with columns and tabs to track characters, gear, origins, dates, and series continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create columns for different attributes (character name, gear, origin, sexuality, etc.) and tabs for different books or data types. Spreadsheets are especially useful for tracking many discrete fields across a series. Lari and Mary describe using Excel to keep details straight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use visual/illustrative boards for imagery and reference
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect images and use slides or boards (PowerPoint, image folders) to supply visual references, especially if you cannot visualize internally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PowerPoint can act as a slide-based reference (one slide per character/technology/location) and store reference photos. This is particularly useful for writers with aphantasia or those who need visual prompts to maintain consistent imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label and categorize notes by function (plot, thread, info)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize notes with labels indicating whether an item is a plot point, a story thread, or background information to be tracked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On notecards, use color-coding or markers to indicate thread type; in digital tools use tags/folders. This helps you keep track of which items need carrying through the manuscript versus which are background notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make unique invented terms easily findable
rubrics_metrics.description: If you invent words or names that are hard to search, create an index or explicit note so you can locate them reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record invented terms separately (with canonical spelling) so search functions will find every occurrence. This prevents inconsistent spellings and missed references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on collaborators (editors, lore keepers) but retain responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Use copy editors or dedicated lore people to collate continuity and produce lists of people/places, but recognize the author remains ultimately responsible for errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professionals may produce a collated list of every mentioned person/location; this is invaluable for continuity. However, authors should verify, because mistakes can still slip through. Mary's anecdote about a continuity error (seven vs. six astronauts) shows the need for personal oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to delete-and-rewrite or clone-and-edit
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose whether you work better by cloning and editing scenes or by deleting and starting fresh when reworking material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some writers (and tools) favor preserving alternate versions for comparison (Scrivener cloning); others find creative benefit in wiping and rewriting. Be explicit about your preferred approach and keep process artifacts (snapshots, copies) if you might need them later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep multiple files / multiple iterations when drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain multiple document versions or files across drafts rather than relying on a single evolving file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dan describes keeping different files for iterations; this can be combined with programmatic version control or manual copies. Helps in case you want to revert to an earlier draft or compare major structural changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use simple drafting environments to reduce friction
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting, consider turning off editor features to create a distraction-free, typewriter-like environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dan turns off features in his word processor so it behaves like a plain typing surface, which can reduce editing impulses while composing. This is a stylistic/tool-use choice to increase output flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audit influences and intentionality of world elements (homework criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine favorite worldbuilding elements and determine their influences and whether their inclusion is intentional and meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Erin's homework: pick ~5 worldbuilding elements, trace their real-world or other-source influences, and ask why they are present and what they bring to the story. This promotes purposeful worldbuilding rather than accidental borrowing.
